title: New 'plant armor' more than triples strawberry yields
summary:
A newly developed textile covering helped strawberry plants produce more than three times as much fruit in tunnel field trials, while showing no harmful effects on plant health. Researchers say the technology may also offer a way to reduce water use and reliance on pesticides in strawberry production.

The fabric, called Plant Armor, is designed to be placed directly over strawberry plants. Its three dimensional structure creates a barrier that keeps insects from reaching the plants, while the layered material still allows sunlight, rain and air to pass through. In tunnel field tests, strawberries protected by Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than uncovered plants. The fabric did not reduce light availability or negatively affect relative humidity.

"To produce fruit, plants need sunlight," said Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant at North Carolina State University and lead author of a paper on Plant Armor. The team had expected the opaque-looking fabric to reduce sunlight and push plants to grow stems and leaves instead of fruit. "However, we found the fabric did not impede access to light at all, and fruit production increased significantly," he said.

Researchers also found that Plant Armor created a steady warming effect throughout the three growing seasons. According to Olawuyi, that extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier than plants grown without the textile. Because Plant Armor physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants, Olawuyi said the technology could also reduce the amount of conventional pesticides needed in agricultural fields.

The idea behind Plant Armor did not begin with farming. The technology emerged from research focused on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and improving comfort for soldiers wearing body armor. That unexpected path demonstrates the value of collaboration across scientific fields, said co-author R. Michael Roe of NC State.

"The path to Plant Armor started with trying to make a cloth to go on a soldier's chest to make body armor more comfortable," said Roe. "We couldn't have predicted that when we started."

The paper is published in the journal Agriculture. The fabric was patented by North Carolina State University and is licensed for commercial development by the university.
why_it_matters: If the results hold up in other tests, farmers could grow more fruit with less reliance on pesticides. The source reports tunnel field trials, so further testing in other settings would still be useful.

questions.question: What did the researchers observe about light and the fabric?
options: It made the light turn red
It blocked most of the sunlight
It only worked at night
It did not reduce light availability
questions.correct_answer: It did not reduce light availability

questions.question: What did the team expect the fabric might cause plants to do?
options: Stop growing completely for a season
Grow many more strawberries than usual
Grow taller than the whole tunnel
Grow stems and leaves instead of fruit
questions.correct_answer: Grow stems and leaves instead of fruit

questions.question: What happened because of the steady warming effect?
options: Covered plants reached the fruiting stage earlier
Covered plants lost all of their flowers
The tunnel stayed cooler than outside
Uncovered plants grew faster than covered ones
questions.correct_answer: Covered plants reached the fruiting stage earlier

questions.question: Why could Plant Armor reduce pesticides, according to Olawuyi?
options: It attracts insects over to other plants
It makes the soil much richer for the plants
It physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants
It keeps rain from ever reaching the roots
questions.correct_answer: It physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants

questions.question: What research did Plant Armor emerge from?
options: Testing new kinds of plant fertilizer
Making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites
Designing better tractors for farms
Studying how wild birds eat fruit
questions.correct_answer: Making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites

questions.question: Who owns the patent for the fabric?
options: A company in Florida
The U.S. Army
The journal Agriculture
North Carolina State University
